claim: Cells constantly adapt to environmental fluctuations.
source: Cells constantly adapt to environmental fluctuations.
evidence: This is a general statement about cellular behavior that is part of established scientific knowledge.

claim: Physiological changes require time and cause a lag phase during which cells do not function optimally.
source: These physiological changes require time and therefore cause a lag phase during which the cells do not function optimally.
evidence: This is a general statement about cellular adaptation that is part of established scientific knowledge.

claim: Past exposure to an environmental condition can shorten the time needed to adapt when the condition re-occurs.
source: Interestingly, past exposure to an environmental condition can shorten the time needed to adapt when the condition re-occurs, even in daughter cells that never directly encountered the initial condition.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction and is a known phenomenon in the field.

claim: History-dependent behavior can occur in daughter cells that never directly encountered the initial condition.
source: Interestingly, past exposure to an environmental condition can shorten the time needed to adapt when the condition re-occurs, even in daughter cells that never directly encountered the initial condition.
evidence: This is a key observation about trans-generational effects that is supported by the literature.

claim: History-dependent behavior in transitions between glucose and maltose does not depend on persistence of proteins involved in metabolism of a specific sugar.
source: In contrast to previous hypotheses, the behavior does not depend on persistence of proteins involved in metabolism of a specific sugar.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Presence of glucose induces a gradual decline in the cells' ability to activate respiration.
source: Instead, presence of glucose induces a gradual decline in the cells' ability to activate respiration, which is needed to metabolize alternative carbon sources.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data including RNA-Seq, Bar-Seq, and protein measurements.

claim: Respiration is needed to metabolize alternative carbon sources.
source: Instead, presence of glucose induces a gradual decline in the cells' ability to activate respiration, which is needed to metabolize alternative carbon sources.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that respiratory activity affects lag phase duration.

claim: Cells adapt to environmental changes by activating and repressing specific genes and processes.
source: In general, cells adapt to such changes by activating and repressing specific genes and processes required to function in the new environment (Brewster et al., 1993; Gasch et al., 2000; Jacob and Monod, 1961; Mitchell et al., 2009a; Perez-Samper et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Physiological re-programming can take a considerable amount of time and resources.
source: Such physiological re-programming can take a considerable amount of time and resources during which the cells do not function optimally, a phenomenon known as the lag phase.
evidence: This is a general statement about cellular adaptation that is part of established scientific knowledge.

claim: Recent exposure to a specific environment can shorten the lag time needed to adapt when the same stimulus re-occurs, even in daughter cells that have not directly experienced the initial change.
source: Interestingly, recent exposure to a specific environment can shorten the lag time needed to adapt when the same stimulus re-occurs, even in daughter cells that have not directly experienced the initial change (D'Urso et al., 2016; Guan et al., 2012; Zacharioudakis et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: History-dependent behavior often extends over several cellular generations.
source: Such HDB often extends over several cellular generations, and is therefore sometimes considered to be a form of rudimentary epigenetic behavior or 'cellular memory'.
evidence: This is a general statement about HDB that is supported by the literature.

claim: History-dependent behavior has been described in various organisms and cell types, ranging from microbes to humans.
source: HDB has been described in various organisms and cell types, ranging from microbes to humans.
evidence: This statement is supported by examples provided in the subsequent text with citations.

claim: Previous exposure to high glucose levels leads to long-lasting stress and damage in pancreatic cells, even after glucose levels have been normalized.
source: One example occurs in pancreatic cells, where previous exposure to high glucose levels leads to long-lasting stress and damage, even after the glucose levels have been normalized, and inversely, prolonged tight control of glycemic values results in lasting improvements, even when glucose levels are not tightly controlled (Tonna et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tonna et al., 2010.

claim: Prolonged tight control of glycemic values results in lasting improvements in pancreatic cells, even when glucose levels are not tightly controlled.
source: One example occurs in pancreatic cells, where previous exposure to high glucose levels leads to long-lasting stress and damage, even after the glucose levels have been normalized, and inversely, prolonged tight control of glycemic values results in lasting improvements, even when glucose levels are not tightly controlled (Tonna et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tonna et al., 2010.

claim: Prolonged changes in blood glucose levels linked to dietary changes may affect muscle and adipose tissue development, even in a next generation that has never been directly exposed to the nutritional stress.
source: Similarly, prolonged changes in blood glucose levels linked to dietary changes may affect muscle and adipose tissue development, even in a next generation that has never been directly exposed to the nutritional stress (Sharples et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sharples et al., 2016.

claim: Trans-generational shift in metabolic state is observed in exponentially growing yeast cells.
source: Furthermore, trans-generational shift in metabolic state is also observed in exponentially growing yeast cells (Slavov et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Slavov et al., 2014.

claim: Changes in chromatin state have been implicated in metabolic programming.
source: The mechanisms underlying metabolic programming have not been fully elucidated, although changes in chromatin state have been implicated in the effect.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: During the lag phase, single-cell organisms arrest their growth, making it easy to observe the adaptation process.
source: HDB is easily studied in single-cell organisms because during the lag phase, these cells arrest their growth, making it easy to observe the adaptation process (Acar et al., 2008; Brickner, 2010; D'Urso et al., 2016; Friedman et al., 2014; Guan et al., 2012; Kundu and Peterson, 2010; Light et al., 2010; Mitchell et al., 2009b; Stockwell et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: When Saccharomyces cerevisiae cells are repeatedly shifted between glucose and galactose, the first shift from glucose to galactose generates a slow induction of the GAL genes with an associated long lag phase.
source: One of the best-documented examples of HDB occurs when Saccharomyces cerevisiae cells are repeatedly shifted between glucose and galactose (Stockwell et al., 2015). The first shift from glucose to galactose generates a slow induction of the GAL genes, with an associated long lag phase.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Stockwell et al., 2015.

claim: When a yeast population is returned to glucose and subsequently switched back to galactose, the GAL induction rate and growth response is significantly faster.
source: When the same population is returned to glucose and subsequently switched back to galactose, the GAL induction rate and growth response is significantly faster.
evidence: This statement describes a known phenomenon in yeast, supported by citations.

claim: History-dependent behavior in glucose-galactose shifts can extend for up to 12 hr after the shift from galactose to glucose.
source: This HDB can extend for up to 12 hr after the shift from galactose to glucose.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the subsequent sentence.

claim: The 12 h-period in glucose during which HDB is retained corresponds to approximately five cellular generations.
source: The 12 h-period in glucose during which the HDB is retained corresponds to approximately five cellular generations, at which point less than 4% of the cells has directly experienced galactose before (Kundu and Peterson, 2010; Sood et al., 2017; Stockwell and Rifkin, 2017; Stockwell et al., 2015; Zacharioudakis et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: A similar phenomenon to glucose-galactose HDB occurs when S. cerevisiae cells are switched between glucose and maltose.
source: A similar phenomenon occurs when S. cerevisiae cells are switched between glucose and maltose (New et al., 2014), and when E. coli cells are switched between glucose and lactose (Lambert et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to New et al., 2014 and Lambert et al., 2014.

claim: A similar phenomenon to glucose-galactose HDB occurs when E. coli cells are switched between glucose and lactose.
source: A similar phenomenon occurs when S. cerevisiae cells are switched between glucose and maltose (New et al., 2014), and when E. coli cells are switched between glucose and lactose (Lambert et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lambert et al., 2014.

claim: Transcriptional induction of genes crucial for rapid growth in the inducing environment are assumed to be the rate-limiting step determining the length of the lag phase.
source: In general, transcriptional induction of genes which are crucial for rapid growth in the inducing environment (e.g. GAL gene induction in galactose) are assumed to be the rate-limiting step determining the length of the lag phase (Lambert et al., 2014; New et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: History-dependent behavior observed at the level of growth is often thought to be linked to a similar effect in the induction of specific genes.
source: As a consequence, HDB observed at the level of growth is often thought to be linked to a similar effect in the induction of specific genes.
evidence: This is a statement about a common assumption in the field, which the authors will challenge.

claim: The regulatory networks governing induction of specific genes are believed to have intrinsic properties that allow faster re-induction if the genes have been recently induced.
source: More specifically, the regulatory networks governing induction of these specific genes are believed to have intrinsic properties that allow faster re-induction if the genes have been recently induced, which in turn leads to a faster resumption of cellular growth (D'Urso et al., 2016; Stockwell et al., 2015; Zacharioudakis et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The assumption that growth resumption is directly governed by the induction kinetics of nutrient-specific genes has not been supported by strong experimental evidence.
source: Importantly, however, the assumption that growth resumption is directly governed by the induction kinetics of nutrient-specific genes has not been supported by strong experimental evidence.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of the existing literature by the authors.

claim: A previous induction of a gene may generate an epigenetically heritable shift in local chromatin structure that allows for quicker re-induction after a short time in the repressive condition.
source: First, a previous induction of a gene may generate an epigenetically heritable shift in local chromatin structure that allows for quicker re-induction after a short time in the repressive condition (Brickner, 2010; Brickner et al., 2007; D'Urso et al., 2016; Tan-Wong et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Protein inheritance or protein perdurance is a proposed mechanism for history-dependent behavior.
source: The second proposed mechanism is the transgenerational persistence of specific proteins, referred to as 'protein inheritance' or 'protein perdurance'.
evidence: This is a description of a hypothesis from the literature.

claim: Proteins needed in one environment do not immediately disappear when cells are shifted to a new environment.
source: This mechanism assumes that proteins needed in one environment do not immediately disappear when cells are shifted to a new environment.
evidence: This is a description of the protein inheritance hypothesis.

claim: During cell division, lingering proteins can be transmitted to the daughter cell and influence how this cell functions, leading to history-dependent behavior.
source: During cell division, some of these lingering proteins can be transmitted to the daughter cell and influence how this cell functions, leading to HDB.
evidence: This is a description of the protein inheritance hypothesis.

claim: Cells growing in galactose have high levels of the galactokinase enzyme Gal1p.
source: Cells growing in galactose have high levels of the galactokinase enzyme Gal1p.
evidence: This is a known fact about yeast metabolism.

claim: When cells are shifted from galactose to glucose, the GAL1 gene is repressed and the Gal1 proteins that were present are gradually diluted as the cells divide.
source: When these cells are shifted to glucose, the GAL1 gene is repressed and the Gal1 proteins that were present are gradually diluted as the cells divide.
evidence: This is a known phenomenon in yeast metabolism.

claim: When cells are shifted again to galactose before cellular Gal1p levels reach a basal level, the remaining Gal1 proteins may allow faster re-induction of the whole set of Gal proteins needed to resume growth.
source: However, when the cells are shifted again to galactose before the cellular Gal1p levels reach a basal level, the remaining Gal1 proteins may allow faster re-induction of the whole set of Gal proteins needed to resume growth (Stockwell et al., 2015; Zacharioudakis et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The causative role of Gal1 protein inheritance has not yet been confirmed.
source: Though these are both plausible mechanisms, it is important to note that the causative role of Gal1 protein inheritance has not yet been confirmed and that environmental shifts can cause much broader changes in transcriptional activity.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of the existing literature by the authors.

claim: Environmental shifts can cause much broader changes in transcriptional activity than just the induction of specific metabolic genes.
source: Though these are both plausible mechanisms, it is important to note that the causative role of Gal1 protein inheritance has not yet been confirmed and that environmental shifts can cause much broader changes in transcriptional activity.
evidence: This is a general statement about cellular responses to environmental changes.

claim: Transitions to glucose stimulate genes involved in fermentation and cellular growth.
source: Transitions to glucose stimulate genes involved in fermentation and cellular growth and repress genes involved in respiration, the glyoxylate and TCA cycles, gluconeogenesis, synthesis of fatty acids and storage carbohydrates, and stress resistance (Conrad et al., 2014; Zaman et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Transitions to glucose repress genes involved in respiration, the glyoxylate and TCA cycles, gluconeogenesis, synthesis of fatty acids and storage carbohydrates, and stress resistance.
source: Transitions to glucose stimulate genes involved in fermentation and cellular growth and repress genes involved in respiration, the glyoxylate and TCA cycles, gluconeogenesis, synthesis of fatty acids and storage carbohydrates, and stress resistance (Conrad et al., 2014; Zaman et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The duration of the lag phase when cells are switched from glucose to maltose depends on the duration of growth in glucose.
source: Specifically, we show that the duration of the lag phase when cells are switched from glucose to maltose depends on the duration of growth in glucose, with longer exposure to glucose eliciting longer lag times.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Longer exposure to glucose elicits longer lag times when cells are switched to maltose.
source: Specifically, we show that the duration of the lag phase when cells are switched from glucose to maltose depends on the duration of growth in glucose, with longer exposure to glucose eliciting longer lag times.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: History-dependent behavior in glucose-maltose shifts does not rely on inheritance of dedicated nutrient-specific proteins (Mal proteins).
source: In contrast to what has been previously suggested, our results show that this HDB does not rely on inheritance of dedicated nutrient-specific proteins (in this case the Mal proteins).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Repression of respiratory pathways during glucose growth and subsequent re-induction upon shift to maltose plays a key role in history-dependent behavior.
source: Instead, several lines of evidence point towards the existence of a much broader mechanism for HDB than previously assumed. Repression of respiratory pathways during glucose growth and the subsequent re-induction upon shift to maltose appears to be playing a key role in HDB.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: Pre-growth in galactose leads to shorter lag in maltose.
source: Firstly, we observe that not only pre-growth in maltose, but also pre-growth in galactose leads to shorter lag in maltose.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: History-dependent behavior is linked to the cytoplasm rather than the nucleus.
source: Secondly, using heterokaryon cells with two nuclei with distinct pre-growth conditions, we show that the HDB is linked to the cytoplasm rather than the nucleus.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 7.

claim: Genes involved in mitochondrial function and respiration play a central role in history-dependent behavior.
source: Thirdly, genome-wide assays show that genes involved in mitochondrial function and respiration play a central role in HDB.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by Bar-Seq and RNA-Seq data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Inhibiting respiration prolongs the lag phase even in cells that only grew for short periods in glucose.
source: Fourthly, inhibiting respiration prolongs the lag phase even in cells that only grew for short periods in glucose.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Over-activating respiration through overexpression of the HAP4 respiratory regulator abolishes history-dependent behavior and results in nearly constant short lag phases.
source: Finally, over-activating respiration through overexpression of the HAP4 respiratory regulator abolishes the HDB and results in nearly constant short lag phases.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: History-dependent behavior is not the consequence of changes in chromatin state or persistence of a few metabolism-specific proteins.
source: Taken together, our data shows that, in contrast to previous suggestions, HDB in changing carbon environments is not the consequence of changes in chromatin state or persistence of a few metabolism-specific proteins.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: History-dependent behavior depends on a much broader metabolic network, with slow changes in respiration and fermentation playing a key role.
source: Instead, the effect depends on a much broader metabolic network, with slow changes in respiration and fermentation playing a key role.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: S. cerevisiae demonstrates strong history-dependent behavior for glucose-to-maltose shifts.
source: Cells demonstrate HDB for the shift between glucose and maltose (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The duration of the lag phase depends greatly on the duration of the preceding glucose growth, with longer glucose exposure leading to longer lag times.
source: Both methods establish that the duration of the lag phase depends greatly on the duration of the preceding glucose growth, with longer glucose exposure leading to longer lag times.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-E.

claim: The increasing lag times are a result of individual cells taking more time to resume growth, as well as an increasing fraction of cells that do not resume growth at all.
source: Interestingly, our single-cell measurements show that the increasing lag times are a result of individual cells taking more time to resume growth, as well as an increasing fraction of cells that do not resume growth at all (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by single-cell experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: History-dependent behavior is not unique to maltose-glucose-maltose shifts.
source: Moreover, this HDB is not unique to maltose-glucose-maltose shifts.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing similar behavior in other carbon source shifts.

claim: A similar history-dependent behavior occurs in galactose-glucose-galactose shifts.
source: We observe a similar behavior in galactose-glucose-galactose shifts and also in glycerol-glucose-glycerol shifts, suggesting that this is a commonly occurring phenomenon (Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: A similar history-dependent behavior occurs in glycerol-glucose-glycerol shifts.
source: We observe a similar behavior in galactose-glucose-galactose shifts and also in glycerol-glucose-glycerol shifts, suggesting that this is a commonly occurring phenomenon (Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: History-dependent behavior is a commonly occurring phenomenon in yeast.
source: We observe a similar behavior in galactose-glucose-galactose shifts and also in glycerol-glucose-glycerol shifts, suggesting that this is a commonly occurring phenomenon (Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of similar behavior in multiple carbon source shifts.

claim: History-dependent behavior is present in L-1374 and BC187, two non-laboratory strains.
source: Finally, we observe that HDB is also present, albeit to different extents, in L-1374 and BC187, two non-laboratory strains (Cubillos et al., 2009) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The intracellular concentration of Mal12p in galactose was approximately 70 times less than its concentration in maltose.
source: In galactose, the intracellular concentration of the maltose-cleaving enzyme, Mal12p, measured using fluorescent protein fusions, was approximately 70 times less than its concentration in maltose, and we were unable to detect the presence of the maltose-transporter Mal1p (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The maltose-transporter Mal1p was undetectable in galactose.
source: In galactose, the intracellular concentration of the maltose-cleaving enzyme, Mal12p, measured using fluorescent protein fusions, was approximately 70 times less than its concentration in maltose, and we were unable to detect the presence of the maltose-transporter Mal1p (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Compared to pre-growth in maltose, pre-growth in galactose increased the timescale over which history-dependent behavior occurs and generally reduced the lag time after short glucose periods.
source: Surprisingly, compared to pre-growth in maltose, pre-growth in galactose actually increased the timescale over which HDB occurs and generally reduced the lag time after short glucose periods.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The observation that pre-growth in galactose reduces lag time after short glucose periods is the opposite of what is expected if inheritance of Mal proteins would be solely responsible for history-dependent behavior after glucose-to-maltose shifts.
source: This is the opposite of what is expected if the inheritance of Mal proteins would be solely responsible for the HDB after glucose-to-maltose shifts.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the experimental data.

claim: Mal proteins are gradually diluted over several generations after a switch from maltose to glucose.
source: Although the Mal proteins are gradually diluted over several generations after a switch from maltose to glucose (Figure 2C), the persistence of the Mal proteins does not cause a shorter lag phase after the shift back into maltose.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The persistence of Mal proteins does not cause a shorter lag phase after the shift back into maltose.
source: Although the Mal proteins are gradually diluted over several generations after a switch from maltose to glucose (Figure 2C), the persistence of the Mal proteins does not cause a shorter lag phase after the shift back into maltose.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: There is little correlation between Mal protein levels and glucose-to-maltose lag duration when cells are first pre-grown in galactose before they are shifted to glucose and then to maltose.
source: Indeed, even though the correlation between Mal12p/Mal11p levels and the population lag time is strong after maltose pre-growth, there is little correlation between Mal protein levels and glucose-to-maltose lag duration when cells are first pre-grown in galactose before they are shifted to glucose and then to maltose (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The observed correlation between Mal protein levels and lag time after pre-growth in maltose only reflects the number of generations of growth in glucose.
source: Therefore, the observed correlation after pre-growth in maltose seems to only reflect the number of generations of growth in glucose.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Galactose pre-growth increased the timescale over which history-dependent behavior occurs and resulted in generally shorter lags compared to maltose pre-growth in glucose-galactose shifts.
source: Galactose pre-growth increased the timescale over which HDB occurs and resulted in generally shorter lags compared to the maltose pre-growth (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is a clear correlation between Gal1p levels and the population lag time after galactose pre-growth.
source: Moreover, whereas there is a clear correlation between Gal1p levels and the population lag time after galactose pre-growth, there is little correlation when cells are pre-grown on maltose (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: There is little correlation between Gal1p levels and the population lag time when cells are pre-grown on maltose.
source: Moreover, whereas there is a clear correlation between Gal1p levels and the population lag time after galactose pre-growth, there is little correlation when cells are pre-grown on maltose (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Pre-growth on maltose, which does not result in measurable Gal1p levels, leads to considerable history-dependent behavior in glucose-galactose shifts.
source: However, pre-growth on maltose, which does not result in measurable Gal1p levels (Figure 2D), also leads to considerable HDB (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2B and 2D.

claim: Gal protein levels are not the major determinants of history-dependent behavior after glucose-galactose shifts.
source: Together, these results suggest that, similar to what we observed for the role of Mal proteins in shifts from glucose to maltose, Gal protein levels are not the major determinants of HDB after glucose-galactose shifts.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Variability in the level of inherited Mal proteins does not explain the variability in single-cell lag times.
source: In both cases, we find that variability in the level of inherited proteins does not explain the variability in single-cell lag times (R2 <0.11).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G, H, I.

claim: Variability in the level of inherited Gal proteins does not explain the variability in single-cell lag times.
source: In both cases, we find that variability in the level of inherited proteins does not explain the variability in single-cell lag times (R2 <0.11).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G, H, I.

claim: There are other factors apart from Mal or Gal protein inheritance influencing the lag time after shifts from glucose to either maltose or galactose.
source: Such absence of a strong correlation further confirms that there are other factors apart from Mal or Gal protein inheritance influencing the lag time after shifts from glucose to either maltose or galactose.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Budding cells are on average 60% more likely to escape the lag at any given time point after the shift.
source: Using the Cox proportional hazard model, we find that budding cells are on average 60% more likely to escape the lag at any given time point after the shift (data point on the x-axis).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The influence of cell cycle stage on single-cell lag times is neglectable.
source: However, this factor on average describes less than 4% of the variability in single-cell lag times (all Cox pseudo-R²<0.094), indicating that the influence of cell cycle stage on single-cell lag times is neglectable.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Cells with different replicative ages were not found to have significantly different lag times.
source: Under this model, cells with different replicative ages were not found to have significantly different lag times.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The variability in single-cell lag times cannot be explained by variability in Mal and Gal protein levels, cell cycle stage, or replicative age.
source: In summary, the variability in single-cell lag times can neither be explained by variability in Mal and Gal protein levels nor by variability in cell cycle stage nor in replicative age.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the experiments.

claim: MAL gene induction dynamics after a glucose-to-maltose shift coincide with the resumption of rapid growth.
source: MAL gene induction dynamics after a glucose-to-maltose shift coincide with the resumption of rapid growth (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Within all observed microcolonies, MAL gene induction is followed by rapid and exponential growth.
source: Within all observed microcolonies, MAL gene induction is followed by rapid and exponential growth and microcolonies that do not induce the MAL genes show little to no growth.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Microcolonies that do not induce the MAL genes show little to no growth.
source: Within all observed microcolonies, MAL gene induction is followed by rapid and exponential growth and microcolonies that do not induce the MAL genes show little to no growth.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: MAL gene induction is preceded by a period of slow growth in many cells.
source: Unexpectedly, we find many cells in which MAL gene induction is preceded by a period of slow growth (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Most microcolonies do not increase more than 2-fold in area before MAL gene induction is detected.
source: However, the amount of growth without MAL gene induction is limited, as most microcolonies do not increase more than 2-fold in area before induction is detected (Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: The mal deletion mutant can enter the slow growth phase but is unable to shift to rapid exponential growth after a shift to maltose.
source: After the shift to maltose, the mal deletion strain is able to enter the slow growth phase but, unlike the wild-type, it is unable to shift to rapid exponential growth (Figure 3B,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and 3D.

claim: GAL gene induction dynamics coincide with the resumption of rapid growth during a glucose-to-galactose shift.
source: During a glucose-to-galactose shift, GAL gene induction dynamics also coincide with the resumption of rapid growth (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Within all observed microcolonies, GAL gene induction coincides with rapid and exponential growth.
source: Within all observed microcolonies, GAL gene induction coincides with rapid and exponential growth, while there is little to no growth in microcolonies not inducing the GAL genes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There is little to no growth in microcolonies not inducing the GAL genes.
source: Within all observed microcolonies, GAL gene induction coincides with rapid and exponential growth, while there is little to no growth in microcolonies not inducing the GAL genes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In contrast to glucose-maltose shifts, a period of slow growth before GAL gene induction is not observed in glucose-galactose shifts.
source: In contrast to glucose-maltose shifts, we do not observe a period of slow growth before GAL gene induction (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: MAL or GAL gene induction is crucial for cells to resume rapid growth.
source: We conclude that MAL or GAL gene induction and the resumption of rapid exponential growth coincide, which is consistent with the idea that MAL or GAL gene induction is crucial for cells to resume rapid growth.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: MAL or GAL gene induction is not necessarily the main determinant of lag phase duration and history-dependent behavior.
source: However, although MAL or GAL gene induction coincides with resumption of rapid exponential growth, this does not necessarily imply that MAL or GAL gene induction is the main determinant of lag phase duration and HDB.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the experimental data.

claim: The slow growth before MAL gene expression suggests that other mechanisms may be the main rate-limiting step for cells escaping the lag phase.
source: In fact, the fact that lag duration does not correlate with Gal and Mal protein levels, and the slow growth before MAL gene expression suggests that other mechanisms may be the main rate-limiting step for cells escaping the lag phase (Figure 3).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The dual MAL11 and MAL12 overexpression strain shows a strongly reduced lag phase.
source: As expected, we find that the dual MAL11 and MAL12 overexpression strain indeed shows a strongly reduced lag phase (Figure 3—figure supplements 4 and 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 4 and 5.

claim: Single overexpression of MAL11 or MAL12 does not result in a strongly reduced lag phase.
source: In contrast, this is not the case when only one of the MAL genes is overexpressed (Figure 3—figure supplements 4 and 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 4 and 5.

claim: After galactose pre-growth, overexpression of MAL12 strongly increases lag time.
source: After galactose pre-growth, overexpression of MAL12 strongly increases lag time, while overexpressing MAL11 slightly reduces the lag time.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: After galactose pre-growth, overexpressing MAL11 slightly reduces the lag time.
source: After galactose pre-growth, overexpression of MAL12 strongly increases lag time, while overexpressing MAL11 slightly reduces the lag time.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: The transporter Mal11p increases the intracellular concentration of maltose, which acts as an inducer of the MAL regulatory network.
source: This result is consistent with their roles in positive and negative feedback loops in the MAL regulatory network: the transporter Mal11p would increase the intracellular concentration of maltose, which acts as an inducer of the network, whereas overexpression of the maltase Mal12p lowers intracellular maltose concentrations by enzymatic breakdown.
evidence: This is an inference based on known biochemical functions of these proteins.

claim: Overexpression of the maltase Mal12p lowers intracellular maltose concentrations by enzymatic breakdown.
source: This result is consistent with their roles in positive and negative feedback loops in the MAL regulatory network: the transporter Mal11p would increase the intracellular concentration of maltose, which acts as an inducer of the network, whereas overexpression of the maltase Mal12p lowers intracellular maltose concentrations by enzymatic breakdown.
evidence: This is an inference based on known biochemical functions of these proteins.

claim: Constitutively high levels of both Mal12p and Mal11p are sufficient to allow rapid resumption of growth after the shift to maltose.
source: Constitutively high levels of both Mal12p and Mal11p are sufficient to allow rapid resumption of growth after the shift to maltose (Figure 3—figure supplements 4 and 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 4 and 5.

claim: There is no correlation between lingering Mal11p and Mal12p proteins prior to a glucose-to-maltose shift in a wild-type strain.
source: However, we also found that there is no correlation between lingering Mal11p and Mal12p proteins prior to a glucose-to-maltose shift in a wild-type strain (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: At least one of the Mal proteins (Mal11 or Mal12) is inherited in a non-functional form during glucose growth in the wild-type strain.
source: Therefore, we hypothesized that in the wild-type strain, at least one of these proteins is inherited in a non-functional form during glucose growth.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental data and previous reports.

claim: Mal11 is rapidly internalized and inactivated after a shift from maltose to glucose.
source: Previous reports indeed suggest that Mal11 is rapidly internalized and inactivated after a shift from maltose to glucose (Görts, 1969; Horak and Wolf, 1997; Jiang et al., 1997; Lucero et al., 2000; Novak et al., 2004; Riballo et al., 1995).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: For the MAL11 overexpression strain, inheritance of native Mal12p elicits minimally short lag times after short glucose periods.
source: This is in fact the case for the MAL11 overexpression strain, where inheritance of native Mal12p elicits minimally short lag times after short glucose periods (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: For the MAL12 overexpression strain, there seems to be little to no effect of native Mal11 protein inheritance, even in a maltose-glucose-maltose transition where the glucose growth is limited to only 2 hr.
source: However, for the MAL12 overexpression strain, there seems to be little to no effect of native Mal11 protein inheritance, even in a maltose-glucose-maltose transition where the glucose growth is limited to only 2 hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 4), suggesting that even if Mal11 proteins are present during glucose growth, they are not able to import maltose, most likely because they have been internalized.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Mal11p and Mal12p levels have the potential to strongly influence the lag time only if both are present at sufficiently high levels and in an active form.
source: In summary, Mal11p and Mal12p levels have the potential to strongly influence the lag time only if both are present at sufficiently high levels and in an active form.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Only the maltase Mal12p is present at high enough concentrations and/or in an active form after glucose growth in wild-type cells.
source: This requirement is not fulfilled in wild-type cells because only the maltase Mal12p is present at high enough concentrations and/or in an active form after glucose growth.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The presence of high levels of both the Mal11 maltose transporter and Mal12 maltase are sufficient for cells to escape the lag phase.
source: So far, our results show that the presence of high levels of both the Mal11 maltose transporter and Mal12 maltase are sufficient for cells to escape the lag phase.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Mal protein inheritance is not the cause of history-dependent behavior during glucose-to-maltose shifts.
source: However, the results also show that Mal protein inheritance is not the cause of HDB during glucose-to-maltose shifts.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: History-dependent behavior must be caused by at least one factor that gradually changes during glucose growth.
source: HDB must be caused by at least one factor that gradually changes during glucose growth.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the observation of HDB.

claim: When the two parents in a mating experiment are grown on the same pre-growth medium (either both in glucose or both in maltose), the resulting diploids and the haploid parental populations demonstrate the same lag behavior.
source: When the two parents are grown on the same pre-growth medium (either both in glucose or both in maltose), the resulting diploids and the haploid parental populations demonstrate the same lag behavior (Figure 3—figure supplement 6, top panels).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: When one parent has been pre-grown on maltose and the other parent is pre-grown on glucose, the resulting diploid demonstrates a lag similar to the parent pre-grown on maltose, and thus has a short lag phase.
source: Interestingly, when one parent has been pre-grown on maltose and the other parent is pre-grown on glucose, the resulting diploid demonstrates a lag similar to the parent pre-grown on maltose, and thus has a short lag phase. (Figure 3—figure supplement 6, bottom panels).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: The diploid has received a high concentration of a growth-promoting factor from the parent that has been grown on maltose.
source: This suggests that the diploid has received a high concentration of a growth-promoting factor from the parent that has been grown on maltose.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The factor determining history-dependent behavior in glucose-maltose shifts promotes growth resumption and is gradually reduced during glucose growth.
source: In other words, this result suggests that the factor determining HDB in glucose-maltose shifts promotes growth resumption and is gradually reduced during glucose growth.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The rate of MAL gene induction is not biased towards one of the two nuclei in heterokaryon cells.
source: We found that the rate of MAL gene induction is not biased towards one of the two nuclei in the heterokaryon cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 7), indicating that the events leading up to MAL gene induction are not restricted to the nucleus, but must involve at least one cytoplasmic step.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 7.

claim: The events leading up to MAL gene induction are not restricted to the nucleus, but must involve at least one cytoplasmic step.
source: We found that the rate of MAL gene induction is not biased towards one of the two nuclei in the heterokaryon cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 7), indicating that the events leading up to MAL gene induction are not restricted to the nucleus, but must involve at least one cytoplasmic step.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: History-dependent behavior is not exclusively due to a transcriptionally poised chromatin structure at the MAL genes.
source: Importantly, this argues against the hypothesis that HDB is exclusively due to a transcriptionally poised chromatin structure at the MAL genes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Deletion mutants with shorter lag phases are enriched for transcriptional regulation, the cytoplasmic ribosome, and histone deacetylation.
source: Deletion mutants with shorter lag phases are enriched for transcriptional regulation, the cytoplasmic ribosome, and histone deacetylation, suggesting that these mutants are defective in gene regulation associated with glucose repression (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by Bar-Seq data and GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Deletion mutants with shorter lag phases are defective in gene regulation associated with glucose repression.
source: Deletion mutants with shorter lag phases are enriched for transcriptional regulation, the cytoplasmic ribosome, and histone deacetylation, suggesting that these mutants are defective in gene regulation associated with glucose repression (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the GO enrichment analysis.

claim: Deletion mutants with longer lag phases are highly enriched for genes involved in respiration and mitochondrial function.
source: More surprisingly, deletion mutants with longer lag phases are highly enriched for genes involved in respiration and mitochondrial function (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by Bar-Seq data and GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The long-then-short mutants contain members of the chromatin modifiers SAS- and SET1/COMPASS-complexes.
source: The long-then-short mutants contain members of the chromatin modifiers SAS- and SET1/COMPASS-complexes.
evidence: This is supported by Bar-Seq data and interaction network analysis.

claim: The short-then-long mutants are enriched for de-novo purine biosynthesis and ESCRT-complexes that are involved in endocytosis.
source: The short-then-long mutants are enriched for de-novo purine biosynthesis and ESCRT-complexes that are involved in endocytosis (Figure 4—figure supplements 4 and 5).
evidence: This is supported by Bar-Seq data and GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 4 and 5.

claim: Genes associated with growth, such as genes encoding elements of the translation machinery are up-regulated during glucose growth and repressed during the lag phase following a shift to maltose.
source: Perhaps not surprisingly, genes associated with growth, such as genes encoding elements of the translation machinery are up-regulated during glucose growth and repressed during the lag phase following a shift to maltose.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The MAL genes are repressed during glucose growth and induced during the lag phase following the shift to maltose.
source: Conversely, the MAL genes are repressed during glucose growth and induced during the lag phase following the shift to maltose.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Genes involved in respiration-related pathways, such as the TCA cycle and the electron transport chain, mirror MAL gene regulation: they are repressed during glucose growth and induced after the shift to maltose.
source: Interestingly, genes involved in respiration-related pathways, such as the TCA cycle and the electron transport chain, mirror MAL gene regulation: they are repressed during glucose growth and induced after the shift to maltose.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The induction of respiration-linked genes precedes the induction of the MAL genes.
source: Moreover, the induction of these respiration-linked genes actually precedes the induction of the MAL genes.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There is a strong induction of genes involved in iron metabolism at the end of glucose growth.
source: There is a strong induction of genes involved in iron metabolism at the end of glucose growth (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2) and processes such as endocytosis, autophagy and proteolysis are up-regulated after the shift to maltose (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: Processes such as endocytosis, autophagy and proteolysis are up-regulated after the shift to maltose.
source: There is a strong induction of genes involved in iron metabolism at the end of glucose growth (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2) and processes such as endocytosis, autophagy and proteolysis are up-regulated after the shift to maltose (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: HAP4 is a central regulator of respiration.
source: Interestingly, among the genes with a gradual repression during glucose (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, bottom left quadrant), we find HAP4, a central regulator of respiration (Lascaris et al., 2003; Lascaris et al., 2004), again hinting at a central role for respiration during the lag phase.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Genes that lead to a long lag when deleted tend to be repressed during glucose growth (repressed on average by 35%).
source: In general, we find that genes that lead to a long lag when deleted tend to be repressed during glucose growth (repressed on average by 35%), whereas genes that lead to a shorter lag when deleted are on average slightly induced during glucose growth (induced on average by 10%) (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of RNA-Seq and Bar-Seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Genes that lead to a shorter lag when deleted are on average slightly induced during glucose growth (induced on average by 10%).
source: In general, we find that genes that lead to a long lag when deleted tend to be repressed during glucose growth (repressed on average by 35%), whereas genes that lead to a shorter lag when deleted are on average slightly induced during glucose growth (induced on average by 10%) (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of RNA-Seq and Bar-Seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Genes that are repressed during glucose growth and lead to long lag when deleted are likely linked to history-dependent behavior.
source: Since we know that the factor determining HDB promotes escape from the lag and is reduced during glucose growth, this first category of repressed genes, which mainly contains genes linked to respiration, is likely linked to HDB.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: There is a good correlation between changes in mRNA levels and protein levels for respiratory genes and MAL genes during glucose growth.
source: The results show that in general, there is a good correlation between changes in mRNA levels and protein levels.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Glucose represses respiration in favor of fermentation even in the presence of oxygen in S. cerevisiae.
source: This is particularly interesting for S. cerevisiae as it is a Crabtree-positive yeast, meaning that glucose represses respiration in favor of fermentation even in the presence of oxygen.
evidence: This is a known characteristic of S. cerevisiae.

claim: The Crabtree effect in yeast resembles the Warburg effect observed in mammalian tumors.
source: This behavior resembles the Warburg effect observed in mammalian tumors (Vander Heiden et al., 2009; Warburg, 1956).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: When cells are shifted from maltose to glucose, the cells reduce their respiratory metabolism gradually.
source: We hypothesized that when cells are shifted from maltose to glucose, the cells reduce their respiratory metabolism, but do so gradually (Slavov et al., 2014).
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: When cells are shifted from glucose to maltose, they need to re-induce respiration to continue growth.
source: When cells are shifted from glucose to maltose, they need to re-induce respiration to continue growth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and known metabolic requirements.

claim: Cells demonstrating higher respiration activity while growing on glucose would have shorter lag times upon a shift to maltose or galactose.
source: This implies that cells demonstrating higher respiration activity while growing on glucose would have shorter lag times upon a shift to maltose or galactose.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the hypothesis.

claim: There is a negative correlation between the level of respiratory proteins in glucose and the lag time.
source: We would therefore expect a negative correlation between the level of respiratory proteins in glucose and the lag time.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the hypothesis.

claim: The expression levels of respiratory proteins (Cit1p, Mdh1p, Kgd2p, Ndi1p, Sdh2p and Cox6p) correlate with the degree of respiration.
source: The expression levels of these proteins have been shown to correlate with the degree of respiration (Fendt and Sauer, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The levels of respiratory proteins correlate well with the population lag times, for pre-growth in maltose and also for pre-growth in galactose (R² between 0.76 and 0.97).
source: Their levels correlate well with the population lag times, for pre-growth in maltose and also for pre-growth in galactose, suggesting that the link between respiration and lag duration is a general phenomenon (R² between 0.76 and 0.97) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The link between respiration and lag duration is a general phenomenon.
source: Their levels correlate well with the population lag times, for pre-growth in maltose and also for pre-growth in galactose, suggesting that the link between respiration and lag duration is a general phenomenon (R² between 0.76 and 0.97) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The correlation between respiratory activity and lag times upon a switch to maltose holds after pre-growth in maltose, as well as after a pre-growth in galactose.
source: Moreover, in contrast to the correlation between population lag times and Mal protein levels (Figure 2E), the correlation between respiratory activity and lag times upon a switch to maltose holds after pre-growth in maltose, as well as after a pre-growth in galactose (Figure 6A.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The transcript levels of COX6 and CIT1 respiratory genes during lag phase is induced to its peak earlier in cells with shorter pre-growth in glucose.
source: Also, consistent with the hypothesis that the ability to induce respiration decreases with residence time in glucose, we observe that the transcript levels of COX6 and CIT1 respiratory genes during lag phase is induced to its peak earlier in cells with shorter pre-growth in glucose (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Only microcolonies that induce respiratory genes show substantial growth.
source: Using our microcolony tracking set-up (Figure 3A), we found that only microcolonies that induce these respiratory genes show substantial growth (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The induction of respiratory genes occurs around the same time as the start of the slow growth period observed within many microcolonies and precedes the induction of the MAL genes by several hours.
source: Interestingly, the induction of these genes occurs around the same time as the start of the slow growth period observed within many microcolonies and precedes the induction of the MAL genes by several hours (Figure 3B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The cross-correlation for Mal11p and Mal12p peaks right after the cells resume growth.
source: The cross-correlation for Mal11p and Mal12p peaks right after the cells resume growth.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The correlation for Cit1p and Cox6p peaks around 4 hr earlier than Mal proteins and is stronger, indicating that expression of these respiratory proteins precedes escape from the lag phase.
source: The correlation for Cit1p and Cox6p, however, peaks around 4 hr earlier and is stronger, indicating that expression of these respiratory proteins precedes escape from the lag phase, whereas, on average, expression of the maltose proteins only occurs around the time of escape.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Altering the respiratory capacity using a chemical inhibitor of respiration (antimycin A) led to substantially longer lag phases and a stronger increase in lag with extended pre-growth in glucose.
source: For both methods, altering the respiratory capacity led to substantially longer lag phases and a stronger increase in lag with extended pre-growth in glucose (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Altering the respiratory capacity using a respiratory deficient mutant (cox6Δ) led to substantially longer lag phases and a stronger increase in lag with extended pre-growth in glucose.
source: For both methods, altering the respiratory capacity led to substantially longer lag phases and a stronger increase in lag with extended pre-growth in glucose (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The HAP4 overexpression strain showed a two-fold decrease in lag duration and a much smaller increase in lag with extended pre-growth on glucose.
source: On average, the HAP4 overexpression strain showed a two-fold decrease in lag duration and a much smaller increase in lag with extended pre-growth on glucose.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The effect of HAP4 overexpression on lag duration occurs both after pre-growth in maltose and pre-growth in galactose.
source: This effect occurs both after pre-growth in maltose and pre-growth in galactose (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: HAP4 overexpression and respiratory deficient mutant (cox6Δ) strains consume oxygen at higher and lower rates respectively, compared to the wild-type.
source: Measurement of dissolved oxygen during lag phase and glucose growth indeed confirms that HAP4 overexpression and respiratory deficient mutant (cox6Δ) strains consume oxygen at higher and lower rates respectively, compared to the wild-type (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Activation of the MAL genes is undoubtedly the final crucial step that allows cells to escape the lag phase.
source: However, while activation of the M﻿AL genes is undoubtedly the final crucial step that allows cells to escape the lag phase, our results suggest that in contrast to what is often suggested, the induction of MAL genes is not the rate-limiting step and that inheritance of Mal proteins or MAL gene expression status does not explain HDB.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The induction of MAL genes is not the rate-limiting step in escaping the lag phase.
source: However, while activation of the M﻿AL genes is undoubtedly the final crucial step that allows cells to escape the lag phase, our results suggest that in contrast to what is often suggested, the induction of MAL genes is not the rate-limiting step and that inheritance of Mal proteins or MAL gene expression status does not explain HDB.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Inheritance of Mal proteins or MAL gene expression status does not explain history-dependent behavior.
source: However, while activation of the M﻿AL genes is undoubtedly the final crucial step that allows cells to escape the lag phase, our results suggest that in contrast to what is often suggested, the induction of MAL genes is not the rate-limiting step and that inheritance of Mal proteins or MAL gene expression status does not explain HDB.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Activation of respiration precedes MAL gene induction.
source: Activation of respiration actually precedes MAL gene induction, and this activation of respiratory metabolism is the main rate-determining step.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Activation of respiratory metabolism is the main rate-determining step in escaping the lag phase.
source: Activation of respiration actually precedes MAL gene induction, and this activation of respiratory metabolism is the main rate-determining step.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The level of respiratory activity has a strong, direct influence on the duration of the lag time and the associated history-dependent behavior.
source: Together, these results show that the level of respiratory activity has a strong, direct influence on the duration of the lag time and the associated HDB.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: History-dependent behavior in maltose-glucose-maltose shifts depends neither on the first encounter with maltose nor on inheritance of Mal proteins.
source: In this work, we provide several lines of evidence indicating that HDB in maltose-glucose-maltose shifts depends neither on the first encounter with maltose nor on inheritance of Mal proteins.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: History-dependent behavior is linked to a previous exposure to any alternative carbon source that requires some degree of respiration, and consequently the gradual decline of respiratory activity during growth on glucose.
source: Instead, the HDB is linked to a previous exposure to any alternative carbon source that requires some degree of respiration, and consequently the gradual decline of respiratory activity during growth on glucose.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The hypothesis that history-dependent behavior is due to a gradual decrease in respiratory activity during glucose growth is consistent with a previous report demonstrating a gradual decrease of respiration over multiple generations in glucose.
source: Our hypothesis that HDB is due to a gradual decrease in respiratory activity during glucose growth is consistent with a previous report demonstrating a gradual decrease of respiration over multiple generations in glucose (Slavov et al., 2014) as well as with a recent study showing the importance of respiration for a switch from glucose to other carbon sources (Perez-Samper et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The hypothesis that history-dependent behavior is due to a gradual decrease in respiratory activity during glucose growth is consistent with a recent study showing the importance of respiration for a switch from glucose to other carbon sources.
source: Our hypothesis that HDB is due to a gradual decrease in respiratory activity during glucose growth is consistent with a previous report demonstrating a gradual decrease of respiration over multiple generations in glucose (Slavov et al., 2014) as well as with a recent study showing the importance of respiration for a switch from glucose to other carbon sources (Perez-Samper et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The mating experiment indicated that history-dependent behavior is caused by a growth-promoting factor that is diluted during glucose growth.
source: The mating experiment indicated that HDB is caused by a growth-promoting factor that is diluted during glucose growth.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The heterokaryon experiment showed that the rate of MAL gene induction is determined by at least a cytoplasmic process.
source: The heterokaryon experiment showed that the rate of MAL gene induction is determined by at least a cytoplasmic process (Figure 3—figure supplements 6 and 7).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The gradual decrease in respiratory activity could be either directly due to protein inheritance of respiratory proteins or complexes during glucose growth, and/or indirectly by the gradual change in an upstream factor determining respiratory activity independently of the respiratory protein levels.
source: The gradual decrease in respiratory activity could be either directly due to protein inheritance of respiratory proteins or complexes during glucose growth, and/or indirectly by the gradual change in an upstream factor determining respiratory activity independently of the respiratory protein levels.
evidence: This is a discussion of possible mechanisms based on the experimental data.

claim: Population-level lag times correlated well with respiratory protein levels.
source: Our population-level lag times correlated well with respiratory protein levels, supporting the former hypothesis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Pre-growth in galactose leads to shorter lag times compared to pre-growth in maltose because the levels of respiratory proteins are higher in galactose than in maltose.
source: Moreover, this could explain the observation that pre-growth in galactose leads to shorter lag times compared to pre-growth in maltose as the levels of respiratory proteins are higher in galactose than in maltose. (Figure 2A–B and Figure 6A).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Upon the sudden loss of glucose, cells enter an energy-deficient state because they are not yet able to metabolize maltose.
source: We hypothesize that upon the sudden loss of glucose, cells enter an energy-deficient state because they are not yet able to metabolize maltose.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: This energy-deficient state would be exacerbated by a decreased respiratory activity in response to glucose.
source: This energy-deficient state would be exacerbated by a decreased respiratory activity in response to glucose: respiration is a more energy-efficient pathway per carbon molecule compared to fermentation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on known metabolic principles.

claim: Respiration is a more energy-efficient pathway per carbon molecule compared to fermentation.
source: This energy-deficient state would be exacerbated by a decreased respiratory activity in response to glucose: respiration is a more energy-efficient pathway per carbon molecule compared to fermentation.
evidence: This is a known fact about cellular metabolism.

claim: The energy-deficient state likely prevents MAL gene induction and subsequent escape from the lag.
source: Finally, this energy-deficient state likely prevents MAL gene induction and subsequent escape from the lag.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: In cells that successfully induce the MAL genes, it is unlikely that MAL gene expression is prevented by the complete depletion of factors that are required for protein expression (e.g. ATP).
source: In cells that successfully induce the MAL genes, it is unlikely that MAL gene expression is prevented by the complete depletion of factors that are required for protein expression (e.g. ATP).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that other proteins are synthesized before Mal proteins.

claim: In cells that successfully induce the MAL genes, protein synthesis of other proteins occurs well before synthesis of Mal proteins.
source: Indeed, in these cells, protein synthesis of other proteins occurs well before synthesis of Mal proteins.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: For the majority of cells that never resume growth, protein expression is inhibited altogether by the depletion of necessary factors.
source: However, it is possible that for the majority of cells that never resume growth, protein expression is inhibited altogether by the depletion of necessary factors.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Cells that never resume growth show no sign of any protein synthesis.
source: Indeed, these cells show no sign of any protein synthesis (Figure 3B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In cells that will eventually induce the MAL genes, MAL gene induction might be prevented until the cells have at least partly recovered from the dip in metabolic flux and ATP production before the energetically costly proton gradient over the cell membrane is used to support maltose import via the H+-maltose symporter.
source: An intriguing possibility is that in the cells that will eventually induce the MAL genes, MAL gene induction might be prevented until the cells have at least partly recovered from the dip in metabolic flux and ATP production before the energetically costly proton gradient over the cell membrane is used to support maltose import via the H+-maltose symporter (Serrano, 1977).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors, supported by a citation about the maltose symporter.

claim: The hypothesis that respiration is required for bridging the energy-deficient state during the lag phase is in agreement with the observation that lag phase in maltose is similar for cultures with pre-growth in maltose or galactose since respiration is active during growth on both sugars and repressed during glucose growth.
source: The hypothesis that respiration is required for bridging the energy-deficient state during the lag phase is in agreement with the observation that lag phase in maltose is similar for cultures with pre-growth in maltose or galactose since respiration is active during growth on both sugars and repressed during glucose growth.
evidence: This is a logical inference connecting the hypothesis to the experimental data.

claim: Previous investigations into history-dependent behavior in carbon sources have not identified the general metabolic state as a central determinant.
source: Previous investigations into HDB in carbon sources have not identified the general metabolic state as a central determinant.
evidence: This is a statement about the existing literature.

claim: Previous studies have noted inheritance of the corresponding metabolic proteins directly involved in either the uptake or processing of the alternative sugars.
source: More commonly, such studies have noted inheritance of the corresponding metabolic proteins directly involved in either the uptake or processing of the alternative sugars (Kundu and Peterson, 2010; Stockwell and Rifkin, 2017; Zacharioudakis et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Previous studies focused on the induction of the genes directly involved in alternative sugar metabolism without showing that induction of these genes is the rate-limiting step in adaptation.
source: Such studies, however, focused on the induction of the genes directly involved in alternative sugar metabolism without showing that induction of these genes is the rate-limiting step in adaptation, and without screening more broadly for processes that may precede and control induction of these genes.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of the existing literature by the authors.

claim: Previous studies did not screen more broadly for processes that may precede and control induction of genes involved in alternative sugar metabolism.
source: Such studies, however, focused on the induction of the genes directly involved in alternative sugar metabolism without showing that induction of these genes is the rate-limiting step in adaptation, and without screening more broadly for processes that may precede and control induction of these genes.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of the existing literature by the authors.

claim: Previous studies revealed a correlation between residual Gal1p levels and the lag duration, but did not show that this correlation implied causation.
source: Although these studies revealed a correlation between residual Gal1p levels and the lag duration, they did not show that this correlation implied causation.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of the existing literature by the authors.

claim: The experimental setups differ between studies, which may influence the main determinants of the duration of lag.
